So I wrote this up because I see a lot of people asking about recipes for their dogs, and since I made my own recipe that is balanced, I figured I'd share with you what I did in case you want to come up with your own recipes based on what you have available to you or you just prefer doing a lot of work in excel versus buying a $6 book...

For the record, I got all of this information on how to formulate a diet from The Possible Canine and K9 Kitchen. I also HIGHLY recommend Canine Nutrigenomics by Dr. Jean Dodds, which includes a list of "canine functional superfoods" that I've also included in my dog's diet. They advocate a precision-based approach by calculating NRC recommendations and determining meats and amounts of meat to meet those recommendations, with supplementation as needed. You don't have to do this; a lot of people don't. But if you're like me and paranoid about taking on your dog's diet at home, this is the guaranteed way to make sure your dog is doing okay. This turns out to be more of a BARF-style diet because I'm adding in starches, veggies, and fruit, as well as heavy supplementation. However, I don't use any bone (besides what is included in the ground turkey/chicken) except duck necks as a weekly treat/dental because I wanted to use ground meats and because there aren't any nutrient breakdowns of bone-in meats and I wanted a more precise approach.

First calculate your dog's daily maintenance energy requirement, which is the number of calories that your dog needs per day. So to do that, figure out your dog's resting energy requirement. The exponential formula, which can be used for dogs of any weight, is:

RER = 70 * (body weight in kg)^0.75

Then you have to figure out your dog's maintenance energy requirement. That will depend on your dog's age, activity level, and whether or not he/she is intact. You find that in Table 9.

My dog is a neutered male, so I used this formula:

MER = 1.6 * RER

So my dog's caloric requirement per day is 1435 calories. The recipe I made is for 1450 calories because he is very active and loses weight easily so he eats a bit more to stay at a healthy weight.

Now the next part is where Excel comes in handy. It's time to calculate your dog's specific nutrient amounts based on his recommended caloric intake. In Table 5, it lists the NRC Nutrient Requirements for Adult Dogs by Minimum or Recommended Allowance. I opt for Recommended Allowance (RA) whenever it's listed. Notice that the nutrient recommendation is per 1,000 calories, so the formula to figure out nutrient levels is:

Nutrient Level = (RA * Calories) / 1000

Also be careful of units. The majority of recommendations in the NRC table is in grams, but the actual amount of nutrients in the ingredients are often listed in mg, so you will have to convert that.

So for example, the recommended amount of calcium is 1,000 mg per 1,000 calories. Using that equation I mentioned above, at 1450 calories, my dog should be getting 1450 mg of calcium from his food. If he doesn't get that much calcium, then I will have to supplement. I like seaweed calcium because it doesn't throw off the phosphorus levels like bone meal does.

So go through that for all of the NRC nutrients listed. I did amino acids, but if you're feeding a meat-based diet, the amino acid levels will be fine. I'm primarily concerned with the minerals, vitamins, lipds, and Ca:P ratio. I also tracked calories, protein, fat, carbohydrates (the consensus seems to be about 20% carbs, give or take based on the dog), and amount of plant matter and amount of meat (Dr. Karen Becker recommends about 25% veggies).

The next step is to determine what ingredients you want to use in your recipe. I use beef liver, beef kidney, beef heart, ground beef, ground turkey, green tripe, and ground chicken. So I used the USDA National Nutrient Database to determine the nutrient levels for each ingredient. I also decided to add canned salmon, eggs, sweet potato, lentils, kale, green peas, blueberries, and goat kefir, so I got the nutritional information for that as well. Make sure that when you select an ingredient, you select the accurate cooking method since that will affect the weight of the product. I use "raw" for all the meat and "cooked" for all the veggies (since I feed the meat raw but use cooked vegetables). I did 1 ounce for everything and set up the excel spreadsheet so I can adjust the amount of the ingredient and it will calculate the exact nutrients for that amount. The formula was referencing cell values so it looks something like this for beef kidney:

Nutrient = 4 mg * (number of ounces in the cell)

I tracked calcium, iron, magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium, zinc, copper, manganese, selenium, and iodine. I also tracked Vitamin C, thiamin (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pantothenic acid (B5), pyridoxine (B6), folate (B9), choline, vitamin B12, vitamin A, vitamin E, vitamin D3, and vitamin K. I also tracked ALA, EPA, and DHA. I also did the amino acids since those were listed as NRC requirements, but I didn't have any problems getting those numbers since his diet is meat-based.

Obviously not all of the ingredients I used had these nutrients, but that's okay because I'm going to supplement specifically what I'm missing. After I set up the spreadsheet, I messed around with the amounts of meat until I got something I was happy with and had the right calories and macros.

So without any supplementation, the diet was deficient in calcium, zinc, iodine, vitamin E, and vitamin D3. The diet was also a little low in EPA+DHA. So I chose to supplement with seaweed calcium to get the right amount of calcium, Kelp Help (contains zinc, iodine, and D3), fish oil (I use Nordic Naturals Omega-3 Pet), and Vitamin E (should always be given whenever you give fish oil). I also add coconut oil.

Now that I had met all of the minimum/recommended nutrient levels, I wanted to ensure that I was not going to overdose him and cause a toxicity, particularly with fat-soluble vitamins. For that, I went to this website that lists the toxic dose of IU per pound of food and compared the toxic dose with what he was getting. He is way under the toxic dose for all of the fat-soluble vitamins. I also calculated the Ca:P ratio, which should be about 1.2:1 to 1.5:1, that I get with seaweed calcium and using whole ground chicken and turkey.

So for those of you who have read all the way to the end and are curious about what his final diet looks like, here it is! Please keep in mind that this is specifically formulated for him, his energy level, and the ingredients that I have, so while I don't mind you taking inspiration from this, copying it directly for your dog could result in nutrient imbalances for your dog (also making a recipe for a smaller dog is not as simple as just halving a larger dog's recipe):

Beef liver, 2 oz

Beef kidney, 2 oz

Beef heart, 4 oz

Canned salmon, 2 oz

Large eggs, 2

Cooked sweet potato, 6 oz

Cooked lentils, 4 oz

Ground beef, 2.5 oz

Ground turkey, 2.5 oz

Green tripe, 2 oz

Ground chicken 3 oz

Cooked kale, 1 oz

Cooked green peas, 1 oz

Blueberries, 1 oz

Goat kefir, 1 oz

Kelp Help, 1 tbsp

Nordic Naturals Omega-3 Pet, 0.5 tsp

Vitamin E, 1 mL (about 200 mg Vit E)

Coconut oil, 1 tsp

Seaweed calcium, 1.5 tsp

Now I was talking all about precision-based nutrition, but I admit that I do mix up the type of veggies that I give him, based on what I have in my freezer or what was on sale. Big Dan's was also out of beef heart, so I am currently using chicken heart that I got from the store, but heart is such a nutrient-dense food that I want to still include it. Otherwise, if I need to vary the amount of meats that I give him, I mess around with it in the Excel spreadsheet that I have so I can make sure that it won't affect the nutrient levels too much (with supplementation, it rarely causes an issue).

And like I said, not everyone has to do it this way. I'm the only one of my friends who does this, and that's okay! I am a big believer in home-prepared diets because of the freshness, variety, and personalization of the diet, but I also am paranoid about any long-term nutrient deficiencies so I want to ensure that he is getting the best possible diet.

We went to the vet yesterday for his vaccinations and bloodwork, and the vet was very happy with his progress and said that he was at a healthy weight and perfect health. She was also relieved that it is all NRC-balanced (obviously vets see a lot of "raw feeding gone wrong") and is a supporter of the homemade diets. My dog doesn't have any health issues, but I wanted to do a precision-based diet because, as raw feeders, we are the pioneers of homemade diets, and I want to make sure that my raw-fed dog is an excellent representative of the diet and that there isn't any room for criticism or deficiency. He also has done extremely well on this diet, with great poops (because that's every raw feeder's barometer), healthy weight, and enough energy to terrorize the lizards in the back yard for hours.

If you have any comments or questions, please let me know! I hope this helps someone!

Belgian doctors to euthanise healthy 24-year-old woman suffering from depression

Although I support euthanasia for people in some cases, Belgium takes things one step too far. She is only 24 and has been living with depression for only 3 years, there is no way that she has "tried everything" to get better yet. She is deciding to go with a permanent solution for a possibly temporary problem.

I am for peoples choices but in this case she is 24 and I was too depressed at that time due to family stuff. This doesn't mean I didn't think of doing it but I realized there was no point of it. I am completely against this. Maybe she needs some life lessons, take her to different parts of the world, live among them, see and learn, maybe then she will realize her mental problems aren't all that to begin with.

Just a slight correction to you stating she's only been living with depression for 3 years, According to the article, it is reported that she has reportedly had "suicidal thoughts" for no less than three years. This means more than 3 years. I think we just don't have enough information about her to make a judgment. Some people (small minority) who suffer from major depression never return to what one would call a normal state, but remain in a constant low level depression called disthymia.

All that being said, I'm not particularly supportive of her decision. She's so young, and I doubt all reasonable treatment options have been explored and tested.
Ok, she's depressed and wants to die. I'm not trying to troll here; why does she need help to kill herself?
Maybe she wants to be certain that the suicide will be without complications. Women are statistically less "successful" at suicides then men. Or maybe the whole thing is cry for help.
It's possible her brain isn't even completely developed yet. I'm afraid this would set a very poor precedent.

She shouldn't be allowed to do it. I always view euthanasia as a good thing to legalize, but that's because my aunt is a oncologist and I've been to the clinic quite a few times. But this just takes it over the top and will probably be used as an example for the 'slippery slope' argument.
You aren't exactly thinking clearly when you are experiencing clinical Depression. The doctors shouldn't allow this.

I don't understand how me choosing to end my life is of concern to ANYONE other than me. I get that family will be sad at the loss, but as long as I don't off myself in a way that could harm others, how does anyone have the right to tell me I can't do it.

It is because depression and thoughts of suicide are often a temporary feeling. I realize your thoughts on its my body and life I will do as I please because i share that belief although any justification for such an early death in a healthy individual is pretty hard for me to support.

You choosing to end your life is one thing.

Asking someone to do it for you is a world of difference, and that's what she is doing here.

While the thoughts of suicide might be temporary, often it is a life long struggle to avoid them without medication and in severe cases WITH medication. And on the subject of medication, sometimes that's worse than the actual depression. My mother-in-law has taken these types of meds for years and she constantly battles with the inability to feel even the most subtle emotions from the most extreme situations. Like being unable to cry at the death of her mother or telling my fiancee that she is upset that she won't be able to cry at our wedding. What is life if your ability to experience it is clear cut because of some drugs you have to take to avoid offing yourself.

You have to look at the perceived value of a life, not the general value of a life. For some people the idea of a life like my mother-in-law's is worse than death itself. It's unfortunate that some people just aren't wired for survival, but who is anyone to tell somebody else that they should have to suffer through a numb existence because "Their life is precious". The system of assisted suicide exist for people to use it and I believe that the choice to live or die is the right of the person who's living or dying.

I was diagnosed with major depressive disorder with suicidal ideations, PTSD, anxiety, and borderline personality disorder at the age of 15. I'm nearly 30 now, but to give context, I DO understand better than most people what enduring lifelong battles with mental illness is like. I deal with it every day.

And when I look at my scars, and think about all the living I almost didn't experience since they were made, I consider life to be worth living. That's precisely why I disagree with euthanasia for otherwise healthy people suffering from depression.

I'm not against euthanasia itself, but I think it's meant for more extreme circumstances, like when you're physically incapable of ending your own life. If she wanted to kill herself and asked that no one try and save her, I'd be OK with that. I wouldn't like it, but I would be OK with it. But her asking someone else to do it for her when she is entirely capable of doing the act herself is the height of selfishness.

That's a really interesting way to look at this. It's is kind of a dick move to make someone else kill you because you can't do it yourself. I'm also glad that you're doing better, but here's the thing. What does one person's life REALLY matter. What is the value that people have put on the act of living. I mean, I get that if they are dead they could have been the one to cure cancer or the one who killed Hitler, but that's a pretty slim chance. Why does one person car if another person they have no connection to is alive or dead. More importantly, why do they care enough that they feel the decision should be put in the hands of government regulation. People are constantly dying all over the world and it has virtually no effect on me.

I know this sounds callous, I'm not a sociopath or anything, I value human life and pretty much life in general. I just think this is an issue of freedom or the lack there of. Some lives are just pain and an unending waterfall of shit. More power to the guy/girl who just wants to check out. It's not like we have a shortage of humans. Plus if the deaths are done in a way that doesn't damage organs or anything then the end of a life that's not wanted could go on to save a life that is wanted.

I suppose in order to make it more palatable, I would be more OK with her saying that her living body is OK to donate to science for whatever testing anyone is willing to do, as long as it inevitably culminates in her death within a reasonable time frame and the process contributes to human knowledge. I get what you're saying, in that the intrinsic value of a life is not necessarily enough to actively prohibit someone from seeking their own death willingly, and you know, when it comes down to it I agree with you.

Essentially, where we disagree is that I don't think it's a dick move to ask someone to kill you if you cannot do it yourself. I think it's a dick move to ask someone to kill you when you are perfectly capable of doing the act yourself. I get asking euthanasia for a quadriplegic who's going to die in a few months anyway--yeah, save them the misery. I'm totally on board with that, and I think taking it a step further I think it would be unethical to force life on someone like that. That's what I mean by this is the absolute height of selfishness--she is entirely capable of hanging herself, or blowing her brains out, or whatever--she does not need someone else to do it for her due to her mental illness. I can say that part safely, beyond a shadow of a doubt, due to my own struggles with mental illness (and thanks for the sentiment on doing better BTW, it's appreciated).

No, I don't think she'll be the one to do something like cure cancer, but I also firmly believe also that a thread has no idea of it's part in a beautiful tapestry. I know that there are tiny moments that happened in my life that tremendously impacted the rest of it, oftentimes with the other person being completely oblivious of just how much of an impact some small gesture/conversation truly had. One thing that really impacted me was watching a documentary about suicide when I was trying to cope with a student who had just done that, it was actually the suicide note from a woman who had jumped from the Golden Gate Bridge. When the police went to her house to investigate, they found her suicide note. It was simple: "Today I'm going to walk to the Golden Gate Bridge. If one person smiles at me, I won't jump."

That woman that died before I was born will never get to know the impact those simple words had on me. How after I went out of my way to make others happy, to smile, and to try and help a stranger whenever I could. She will never know how two simple sentences changed my entire outlook on life itself.

Circling back to our conversation though, I must say I disagree further that it's an issue of freedom or lack thereof. No one is telling her she's not allowed to kill herself, they and I are saying we have a problem with her asking someone else to do it. That impacts other's freedoms, and worse, might lead to sanctions against euthanasia as a whole and actually deprive innocent people who are far more deserving (and actually incapable) of receiving it. It's great that she has managed to start more worldwide conversations about the ethical ramifications of this altogether, but I feel that it might negatively impact and sour people's views on the entire concept, and for that reason alone I think her request should be denied.

I feel you. The assisted suicide conversation is going to be the abortion conversation of the next few years. Let me clarify my statement, when I said someone who "cannot" I meant someone who doesn't have the gumption to actually kill themselves even though they want to die. I've never been suicidal but I imagine there is a lot of fear that comes along with the decision to off yourself and I also imagine that that fear could be a kind of torment. I want to die, if only I could pull this trigger or kick this stool or pull this blade through my vein. I guess what I'm trying to say is that sometimes people need help with unsavory task (like killing yourself) and it doesn't deminish their desire to die, they just need help. Like that hypothetical quadriplegic, he's prevented from killing himself by lack of limbs. This woman could be prevented from killing herself by lack ability to actually do the deed. I don't think she should be made to feel her struggle isn't real enough to get the help she need.

As to the freedom side of things, I take a firm belief that my life is mine to do with as I please and I'm very protective of the freedom I have with that life. What I eat/do/feel is the last bastion of freedom I have in this world. So if an action is only going to affect me and my very small sphere of influence then I don't think I should be prevented from doing that action, especially not by a government agency.

Also on a completely unrelated note. This conversation could never have happened on reddit. Cheers and thanks for the debate!

Freedom is also sacrosanct to me, but personal freedom must not extend to the point that it interferes with the freedom of others. It's important in this debate to remember consequences. If a doctor is willing to perform euthanasia on a patient with depression, it will dramatically change the scope of the work he's able to do. That's a tarnished doctor, he or she would be a pioneer--the first of their kind. And not in a good way.

Sometimes, I still struggle and need to reach out for help. But if a quick google search reveals a psychiatrist is going to be willing to kill me for my depression--I can tell you unabashedly I would not even begin to consider going with that doctor under any circumstances. As a parent, if my child needed psychiatric help and a google search revealed that? Fuck no my child wouldn't be going to that doctor, I'd take him to a different one. As such, the only patients he or she will attract will be patients who's only intent is to ask that doctor to be the next Kevorkian. How is that fair to that doctor's freedom? A doctor who will make their career not be about preserving life, but about taking it instead?

What about when in other countries that try and push for merciful euthanasia laws? Too bad, she will be the poster child of anti-euthanasia protesters. Her face will be associated with why it's bad to allow it, and it would be incredibly naive to think that that wouldn't impact other politicians' decisions on whether or not to allow it. What a terrible thing to even contemplate--that achieving your death through others would guarantee that others who were incapable of taking their own lives would be forced to live, despite how unethical it is to force those others to live in their circumstances.

It's important to explore the ethical ramifications here, and the future impact this precedent will set. If it's allowed, it could make euthanasia be perceived as barbaric in any circumstances, and that's horrific. She will set the crusaders who try and advocate for euthanasia back 50 years. That alone should give us a significant amount of pause when regarding this.
Horribly unethical in every way. I guess medical science has just given up trying to actually cure or treat stuff and are just going to start killing people.
This is going to sound really cold and maybe it is but I say let her go. The world is heavily over-populated and if you don't want to be here sucking up resources, then don't.
